title: Proving Japanese Ability for a Student Visa: The 2026 Requirement Explained
summary: A record of 150 study hours no longer proves your Japanese at the visa stage. You now need a test certificate or an interview — and the interview is scored.
body_html:
Until 2026, a school could evidence your Japanese by stating you had completed 150 hours of study. [source:1] That was enough to establish A1-level ability at the application stage. [source:1]

It is no longer accepted. A test certificate, or confirmation by interview, is now required. [source:1]

This is already in force, not upcoming. Both dates below have passed.

Which applications it applies to, and from when [source:1]

The change lands in two parts. [source:1]

  • Certificate of Eligibility applications: applies to students planning to enrol from October 2026 onwards. [source:1]
  • Change-of-status and extension applications: applies to applications filed from 1 July 2026. [source:1]

It also covers Japanese-language departments attached to universities, not only standalone language schools. [source:1]

What the interview actually consists of

This is the part worth reading closely, because the agency published the wording it wants schools to use when recording the result — and that wording describes the mechanics.

For an interview, the example reads: the Japanese required for admission is A1-equivalent on the reference framework; A1-level questions were asked in Japanese during the interview; the applicant answered a given number correctly out of a given number, in Japanese; the pass threshold was a given number of correct answers. [source:1]

For a written test, the example reads the same way with a score instead of a count. [source:1]

Three things follow from that, and none of them appear in the usual advice.

You will be asked questions in Japanese and expected to answer in Japanese. Not asked about your motivation in English, with Japanese mentioned in passing. The recorded result is a count of correct Japanese answers.

There is a numeric pass threshold. The school sets it, but it exists and gets written down. "I did my best in the interview" is not what goes on the form; a number does.

The level is A1. [source:1] That is the entry level of the reference framework — introducing yourself, basic everyday exchanges. It is not a high bar. But it is a bar, and it is now checked rather than inferred from an attendance record.

The form your school fills in

The school completes a confirmation form and submits it with your application. [source:1] One of two boxes must be ticked: test, or interview. [source:1] The agency asks that the method be described in detail and objectively, which is why the example wording is so specific. [source:1]

Two practical details most people miss.

If your Japanese is evidenced by a test certificate, that certificate must be submitted with the application — regardless of whether your school is on the approved-institution list. [source:1] Being at a well-regarded school does not exempt the paperwork.

And if your school has not changed since your previous application, the confirmation form is not required again. [source:1] For an extension at the same institution, this is one less thing to chase.

A test certificate does not replace the interview

Even where a test certificate exists, schools are asked to interview the applicant wherever possible, and to confirm Japanese ability properly during that interview. [source:1]

So holding a JLPT or equivalent result does not mean you skip the conversation. Treat the certificate as removing a risk, not removing a step.

One exemption

Applicants who hold the nationality of a country or region on the agency's published list, who graduated from a higher education institution abroad and submit the graduation certificate, are not required to evidence Japanese ability at all. [source:1]

Whether your nationality is on that list is not something to guess at — the list is published by the agency and your school will know. Ask before you book a test you may not need.

What to do

  • Ask your school which route they are recording for you: test certificate, or interview. [source:1] One of the two has to be on the form.
  • If it is the interview, ask what their pass threshold is. They have one, because they have to write it down. [source:1]
  • Prepare to answer basic questions in Japanese, not about Japanese.
  • If you already hold a test result, send it to the school early — it has to go in with the application. [source:1]
  • Extending at the same school? Confirm whether the form is needed at all. [source:1]

This change arrived alongside a second one in the same notice, covering how schools monitor student part-time work. If you are working or plan to, see what actually changed about the part-time work rules.

Applications are assessed case by case and the official notice is the only authority. It is linked below. This page summarises it; it does not advise.

sources.publisher: 出入国在留管理庁（Immigration Services Agency of Japan）

claims_without_sources: A1 が「自己紹介や基本的な日常のやりとり」の水準であるという説明 —— 日本語教育の参照枠の一般的な定義であって、本通知に書かれているわけではない。通知は「Ａ１相当」としか言っていない。読者が水準を掴めないと記事の意味がないため説明は入れたが、出典マーカーは付けていない。
「JLPT」という具体的な試験名 —— 通知は「試験の証明書」としか書いておらず、特定の試験を指定していない。本文でも例示として触れるにとどめ、要件であるかのようには書いていない。
別表掲載国・地域の具体的な国名 —— 当庁 HP の別表を確認していないため列挙せず、「学校に聞け」とした。
面接で不合格になった場合に何が起きるか —— 通知に記載がない。推測で書かない。
学校が設定する合格基準の具体的な水準 —— 通知は記載例に「〇問」と空欄を置いているだけで、数値を定めていない。したがって「基準は存在し記録される」とだけ述べ、相場を示唆する書き方はしていない。
